questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Define GDP as market value of final goods
questions.stem: A dispatcher's log records total market value of all final goods produced domestically in a quarter

options.text: This measure is gross domestic product
This measure is gross national product

questions.explanation: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period. The domestic boundary and final goods define it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log shows 100 dollars of steel sold to a car maker and 1000 dollars of cars sold to buyers

options.text: Zero counts because steel is domestic

questions.explanation: Intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting. Only the 1000 dollars of final cars enters GDP.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute value added at a stage
questions.stem: A dispatcher notes a mill sells flour for 200 dollars after buying wheat for 120 dollars; what is value added
questions.explanation: Value added equals 200 minus 120, which is 80 dollars. Summing value added across stages yields GDP.
questions.hint: Subtract input cost from output value

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Value added and the final good
questions.learningObjective: Show value added sums to final value
questions.stem: Explain why summing value added across stages equals the final good's value

answer.exemplar: Each stage's value added is its output minus purchased inputs, so intermediate values cancel and only the final good's total value remains.

questions.explanation: Value added nets out intermediate purchases at each stage. Summing leaves the final good's full market value.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log records a used locomotive resold for 50000 dollars

options.text: The resale counts as new output
The resale is excluded from GDP
The resale counts at half value

questions.explanation: Second-hand sales are excluded because the good was counted when first produced. Only broker commissions on the sale count.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A dispatcher's log groups spending into consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports

options.text: These are the income components of GDP
These are the expenditure components of GDP

questions.explanation: GDP by expenditure equals consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports. These four components sum to total output.
questions.hint: Match to C plus I plus G plus NX

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log shows 30000 dollars spent on new rail cars and 5000 dollars on fuel

options.text: Only the rail cars count as investment
Neither counts because both are expenses

questions.explanation: New rail cars are capital goods, so they count as investment. Fuel is an intermediate input consumed in production, not investment.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a government pension payment is not a government purchase in GDP

answer.exemplar: A pension is a transfer payment with no good or service produced in return, so it is excluded from government purchases and GDP.

questions.explanation: Government purchases require production of goods or services. Transfers redistribute income without production, so they are excluded.
questions.hint: Ask if a service was produced

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log shows exports of 20000 dollars and imports of 15000 dollars; what are net exports
questions.explanation: Net exports equal exports minus imports, so 20000 minus 15000 is 5000 dollars. Imports are subtracted because they are not domestic production.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A dispatcher's log adjusts output for price changes to measure true volume

options.misconception: confuses output measure with price index

questions.explanation: Real GDP values output at constant prices, removing price changes. It measures true volume of production.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log shows nominal output rose 8 percent while prices rose 3 percent
questions.explanation: Real growth approximates nominal growth minus inflation, so 8 minus 3 is about 5 percent. Prices inflated part of the nominal rise.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain what the GDP deflator measures

answer.exemplar: The GDP deflator measures the price level of all domestically produced final goods and services, comparing nominal to real output.

questions.explanation: The deflator is a broad price index for domestic output. It converts nominal GDP into real GDP.
questions.hint: It is a price index for domestic output

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Nominal GDP is 1100 dollars and real GDP is 1000 dollars; compute the GDP deflator
questions.explanation: The deflator equals nominal divided by real times 100, so 1100 over 1000 times 100 is 110. It is an index with base 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The GDP deflator rose from 100 to 105; what is the inflation rate
questions.explanation: Inflation equals (105 minus 100) divided by 100 times 100, which is 5 percent. The deflator change measures price growth.
questions.hint: Compute percent change in the index

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Limits of real growth as a welfare measure
questions.stem: A log shows real GDP rose but pollution and leisure are ignored

options.text: Real GDP growth equals welfare growth
Real GDP growth overstates welfare gains
Pollution raises GDP so welfare is fine

questions.explanation: GDP omits pollution, leisure, and distribution. Rising real GDP can overstate welfare improvements.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log shows GDP of 1000000 dollars and population of 10000
questions.explanation: Output per person equals GDP divided by population, so 1000000 over 10000 is 100 dollars. It approximates average living standards.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain the income approach to measuring output

answer.exemplar: The income approach sums wages, rents, interest, and profits earned in producing output, which equals the value of output produced.

questions.explanation: Income earned in production equals the value of output. Wages plus rents plus interest plus profits sum to GDP.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log notes underground activity is missed by official GDP

options.text: This causes GDP to be overstated
This has no effect because underground is zero
This causes GDP to be understated

questions.explanation: Unmeasured underground production means official GDP understates true output. Measurement error is unavoidable in national accounts.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log shows GDP of 5000 dollars and depreciation of 300 dollars
questions.explanation: Net domestic product equals GDP minus depreciation, so 5000 minus 300 is 4700 dollars. Depreciation is capital consumption.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain gross national product

answer.exemplar: Gross national product is the market value of final goods produced by a country's residents anywhere in the world, including income from abroad.

questions.explanation: GNP uses the national boundary rather than the domestic boundary. It adds net factor income from abroad to GDP.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A log records a quarter's domestic final output of 8000 dollars; what does this represent

options.text: It represents GNP for that quarter
It represents GDP for that quarter

questions.explanation: Domestic final output in a quarter is GDP. The domestic boundary and period define the measure.

questions.stem: Consumption 400, investment 100, government 150, exports 80, imports 60; compute GDP

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Gross investment is 500 dollars and depreciation is 120 dollars; what is net investment
questions.explanation: Net investment equals gross investment minus depreciation, so 500 minus 120 is 380 dollars. It measures addition to capital stock.

options.text: Net exports are zero because both are large

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Nominal GDP is 1200 dollars and the deflator is 120; compute real GDP
questions.explanation: Real GDP equals nominal divided by deflator times 100, so 1200 over 120 times 100 is 1000 dollars. Constant prices remove inflation.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain nominal rise with flat real output
questions.stem: Explain why nominal GDP can rise while real GDP is flat

answer.exemplar: Nominal GDP rises with prices even if physical output is unchanged, so real GDP, which holds prices constant, stays flat.

questions.explanation: Nominal GDP uses current prices, so price increases raise it without more output. Real GDP removes price effects.
questions.hint: Prices can rise without more output

questions.explanation: GDP ignores non-market activity and distribution. Growth in average output need not mean better welfare for all.

questions.stem: Explain why counting both steel and cars would overstate GDP

questions.explanation: Intermediate values are embedded in final prices. Counting both inflates output by the intermediate amount.
